observations: ct-tag-list itself renders no images. Each composed ct-tag's optional icon (via ct-icon) is always decorative/aria-hidden and accompanies the tag's own required visible `content` text, so it is never this component's sole source of non-text content. Compliance depends on the implementer providing meaningful text alternatives for any non-text content placed in the free-form `content-top`/`content-bottom` slots.
ct-tag-list renders no audio or video.

standard: 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A)

observations: Every ct-tag-list-item child is composed as a real <li class="ct-item-list__item"> inside a <ul class="ct-item-list"> (via the internally-composed ct-item-list), giving assistive technology accurate list/listitem role and item-count information regardless of how many tags are supplied or what each tag contains. Establishing that structure is inherent to composing ct-item-list, so this is met unconditionally rather than depending on the implementer to add it separately.

Tags render in the same order their ct-tag-list-item children appear in the DOM; neither ct-tag-list nor the composed ct-item-list ever use the CSS `order` property to reassign visual order, so reading/visual order always matches DOM order.
ct-tag-list issues no instructions that rely on shape, size, or visual location to be understood.
The composed ct-item-list's horizontal, wrapping layout is a design choice, not a device-orientation restriction; content is not locked to a single display orientation.
ct-tag-list renders no form inputs.

`content` is a required attribute on every ct-tag-list-item, and ct-tag always renders it as visible text — the primary/secondary/tertiary variant's background/border color differences supplement that text rather than substituting for it, so no tag ever conveys meaning through color alone.

Every composed ct-tag reuses ct-tag's own light/dark color tokens (already verified against a 4.5:1 minimum in wcag-data/tag.json) for all three variants, so tag text contrast is already covered. Compliance for any content placed in the `content-top`/`content-bottom` slots is the implementer's own responsibility, same boundary as ct-publication-card's equivalent slots.

Tag text uses rem-based typography tokens and the composed ct-item-list's `flex-wrap: wrap` lets tags reflow onto additional lines as text grows at 200% zoom, rather than clipping or requiring horizontal scrolling.
ct-tag-list renders no images of text; every tag's content is real, selectable text.
The composed ct-item-list's `flex-wrap: wrap` means tags wrap onto new lines instead of requiring two-dimensional scrolling at a 320px-equivalent viewport.

Each composed ct-tag's own border colors already meet the 3:1 minimum per wcag-data/tag.json. However, url-bearing tags render as focusable `<a>` elements and ct-tag's compiled `:focus-visible` rule (unchanged by this port — see the 2.4.7 entry below) defines no outline or other visible focus indicator at all, so there is no focus-indicator contrast to evaluate for link tags — the indicator is simply absent, not merely low-contrast.

Neither ct-tag-list nor the composed ct-item-list/ct-tag impose a fixed-height or `overflow: hidden` container that would clip text when line-height/letter-spacing/word-spacing are increased to the criterion's minimums.

standard: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus (Level AA)
observations: ct-tag-list introduces no hover/focus-triggered content of its own (no tooltips or popovers).

url-bearing tags render as native `<a>` elements (via ct-tag), which are natively keyboard-operable with no custom widget behavior layered on top. Plain (non-link) tags are not interactive and require no keyboard operation.
No custom focus management is introduced; native anchor focus behavior applies to any url-bearing tag.

standard: 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold (Level A)

observations: As with 1.3.2/2.1.1, tags are never reordered visually via CSS `order`, so any focusable (url-bearing) tags receive focus in an order matching both the DOM and the visual layout.

Compliance depends on the implementer supplying a `content` value that is itself a clear, descriptive link label for any url-bearing tag (e.g. a topic name like "Transport" rather than "click here") — ct-tag-list has no separate link-text prop to check against; `content` doubles as both the visible label and the accessible name for link tags.

ct-tag-list renders no headings or form labels of its own; each tag's `content` is evaluated under 2.4.4 (link purpose) instead, since a tag is a categorization label/link, not a heading or form label.

Plain (non-link) tags are not focusable, so this criterion does not apply to them. For url-bearing tags: ct-tag (already-merged, separately-owned 01-atoms/tag component, unchanged by this port — same boundary drawn in ct-social-links's doc comment) compiles its `:focus-visible` rule to only `text-decoration: none`, with no `outline`/`box-shadow` of any kind. A keyboard user tabbing through a tag-list containing url-bearing tags currently gets no visible focus indicator on any of them. This is a genuine gap in the composed ct-tag component, not something an implementer using ct-tag-list can fix from the outside — flagged here and in this port's summary for follow-up on ct-tag itself, rather than silently rated Pass or worked around in this component.
ct-tag-list introduces no sticky/overlaying content that could obscure a focused tag.
url-bearing tags use the native anchor click event, which already honors standard cancellation (e.g. moving the pointer away before release aborts the activation).

A url-bearing tag's accessible name is its `content` text (rendered as both the visible label and the anchor's `title`/text content by ct-tag) — the visible label and accessible name are always identical, so this is met unconditionally rather than depending on the implementer.

Target size for a url-bearing tag's clickable area is entirely a property of the composed ct-tag component (its own padding/font-size), not something ct-tag-list adds to or constrains — deferred to ct-tag's own audit rather than duplicated here, same delegation item-list.json uses for slotted-content concerns.
Compliance depends on the implementer setting the correct `lang` attribute on the page's `html` element, not on this component.

Compliance depends on the implementer setting a `lang` attribute on a tag's content (or on content-top/content-bottom slot content) when its language differs from the page's — ct-tag-list has no mechanism of its own to set this.
Focusing a url-bearing tag triggers no context change beyond native anchor focus; ct-tag-list adds no focus-triggered side effects.
ct-tag-list has no input props that trigger behavior — `theme`/`vertical-spacing` only affect layout/color, never navigation or context, and per-tag props are static data, not live input.
Compliance depends on the implementer using the same variant/icon conventions for the same kind of tag consistently across the site (e.g. always marking external destinations with `external`).
ct-tag-list is not a form control and produces no validation errors.
ct-tag-list is a categorization/navigation display, not a form control; it provides no input labels or instructions.

The composed ct-item-list's native <ul>/<li> elements automatically expose "list"/"listitem" roles (with correct position-in-set/set-size) without custom ARIA, and each url-bearing tag is a native <a> whose name/role/value come from the browser for free. Non-link tags are plain <span> elements carrying only their own visible text, requiring no additional role.
ct-tag-list has no dynamic/live-updating behavior of its own — it renders once from its children with no state changes to announce.
